questions.q: What is the real tradeoff of using WITH COMPRESSION on a backup?
options: The backup file becomes smaller, but compression is CPU-bound work that can increase backup time on a CPU-constrained server
Compression makes backups larger but faster to create
Compression eliminates the need for a full backup
Compression has no measurable effect on backup size or CPU
questions.explain: Compressed backups are typically 50-70% smaller, but the compression work itself competes for CPU with production queries on the same server.

questions.q: What must exist before a backup can use the ENCRYPTION option?
options: A certificate or asymmetric key must already exist in the target database (typically master) for the backup to reference
Nothing — ENCRYPTION can be added to any BACKUP statement with no prerequisites
The database must first be converted to SIMPLE recovery
A separate encrypted disk volume must be provisioned
questions.explain: Encryption isn't a standalone flag — the BACKUP statement's ENCRYPTION clause references a certificate (via CREATE CERTIFICATE) or asymmetric key that must already exist.

questions.q: Why is running BACKUP CERTIFICATE considered a step nobody can skip, per this lesson?
options: The certificate is the only thing that can decrypt the backup later — if it's lost, every encrypted backup it protected becomes permanently unrestorable
BACKUP CERTIFICATE is required by SQL Server before any BACKUP DATABASE statement will run
It has no real consequence if skipped, since certificates are automatically recoverable
It only matters for backups stored on a network share
questions.explain: A lost, un-backed-up certificate makes its encrypted backups permanently unreadable, even though the .bak file itself remains intact.

questions.q: Per this lesson, when does backup compression most clearly earn its cost?
options: When the backup destination is network-bound (a share, remote datacenter, or cloud storage) or when local disk space for retention is tight
Only when the database is set to SIMPLE recovery
Compression never earns its cost and should always be avoided
Only on databases smaller than 1 GB
questions.explain: A smaller file transfers meaningfully faster over a network-bound path and eases tight storage budgets — that's where compression's CPU cost pays off most.

questions.q: A DBA creates a certificate and encrypts a database's backups the same day, but never runs BACKUP CERTIFICATE. Six months later the server is rebuilt from scratch. What happens when they try to restore one of the encrypted backups?
options: The restore fails — without the certificate backed up and restored to the new server first, the encrypted backup cannot be decrypted
The restore succeeds normally because SQL Server regenerates certificates automatically
The backup file automatically decrypts itself if no certificate is found
Encrypted backups don't require a certificate to restore, only to create
questions.explain: Since the certificate was never backed up, it doesn't exist on the rebuilt server, and the encrypted backup has no key available to decrypt it — a permanent loss.
